<reason>A more convincingly defended the actual rule, distinguishing meaningful scrutiny from signatures and payment restoration from repairing harm. B raised a serious counterexample involving imminent fraud and unavailable reviewers, and offered responsive hardship safeguards. But B weakened that challenge by repeatedly treating suspected hijacking as established theft and comparing its preferred system against queues and rubber stamps that A expressly prohibited. A answered the implementation pressure with auditable review criteria and honestly acknowledged the remaining fraud-prevention cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s second rebuttal dismantled B’s central queue comparison: withholding an existing benefit pending review solely because of a flag already violates the proposed rule. A also clarified that meaningful review can reach a mistaken outcome, defeating B’s accusation that the definition simply excludes every failure.</best_rebuttal>
